title: Detection of Virtual Private Server
summary: This detection strategy looks for evidence that an adversary is using a rented virtual private server as staging, relay or command and control infrastructure, and for signs that a virtual private server belonging to your organisation has been taken over. The technique covers both buying a server from a hosting provider with criminal funds and compromising somebody else's server. The telemetry that makes it visible is cloud audit logging for instance creation, network flow records that show long sessions to hosting provider address space, and domain name system lookups for dynamic names hosted there. In practice the strategy fails because content delivery, update services and remote support all look the same on the wire, so an analyst needs asset inventory and provider ownership data before a session can be judged.

beginner.definition: A virtual private server is a computer that you rent from a hosting company. It runs on shared hardware but behaves like a machine of its own. Attackers rent these servers to store tools, relay traffic and hide their true location. This detection looks for traces of that use in your cloud and network logs.
beginner.whyItMatters: You cannot investigate a threat that you cannot see. Attackers often pay for these servers with stolen payment cards. The rental therefore leaves no obvious link to a real person. From that server they can send phishing mail or scan your network. Some attackers also use it to keep control of a machine inside your company. When your team sees a session to a hosting address, it must judge the intent. That judgement decides whether you cut the link or watch it quietly.
howItWorks: Your cloud provider writes an audit record whenever someone creates a virtual machine inside your account.
The detection reads those records and checks who created the machine, from where, and at what time.
Separately, network flow logs record every session that leaves your network and the address it reached.
An enrichment table maps each address to the organisation that owns it, such as a hosting provider.
Long sessions that send a small, steady amount of traffic to a hosting address score higher than short bursts.
When a session matches the pattern, the rule raises an alert and attaches the account and the host name.
beginner.example: Imagine a night watchman who guards your building. He cannot see inside the rented storage unit across the street. But he can see a cable that runs from your back door to that unit. He also notices that a visitor goes there every night at the same time. The cable alone proves nothing, because a delivery van also stops there. So the watchman writes down the time, the unit number and the visitor description. Then he asks the manager who rented that unit. Your detection works in the same way. It cannot see the attacker. So it collects the links that point at the rented server and asks a human to judge them.
takeaways: Rented servers are cheap and hard to trace, so attackers use them as a base.
Your own cloud audit logs show every machine created inside your account.
Flow records plus owner lookups turn a strange address into a useful clue.

objectives: Explain what a virtual private server is and why an attacker would rent one.
Name the telemetry sources that show virtual private server abuse.
Describe how to join network flow records with address ownership data.
Recognise the legitimate traffic that looks like this pattern.
Decide when a session to a hosting provider deserves escalation.
dataSources: Cloud provider audit logs for virtual machine creation, with caller identity, source address and region
Network flow records such as NetFlow or IPFIX, with destination address, byte counters and session duration
Domain Name System query logs for lookups of dynamic names hosted on provider address ranges
Address ownership and autonomous system enrichment tables built from routing registry data
Abuse or takedown reports sent to your security team by hosting providers and law enforcement
logic: The pattern is a long lived outbound session from an internal host to an address owned by a hosting provider, especially when the same address is contacted on a regular schedule. The fields that must be correlated are the internal source address, the account or process that opened the session, the destination address and the autonomous system that owns it, and the session duration and byte volume. Benign traffic to hosting providers is common, because content delivery, software updates and remote support all run there. The malicious case is distinguished by regularity with no business reason, a destination that no asset inventory record claims, and a session that continues after the user has logged off.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Long Outbound Session to Hosting Provider Address Space
# logsource:
#   product: network
# detection:
#   selection:
#     direction: 'outbound'
#     dst_asn_owner: 'hosting_provider'
#     duration_seconds: '> 1800'
#   filter_approved:
#     dst_ip|in: 'approved_service_endpoints'
#   condition: selection and not filter_approved
# level: medium
falsePositives: Content delivery and software update traffic that terminates on hosting provider address ranges.
Sanctioned remote support sessions started by an approved third party vendor.
Developer workstations that connect to cloud instances in the company own tenancy.
Backup or replication jobs that push data to an off site storage provider.
tuningNotes: Baseline every internal host that talks to hosting provider address ranges for more than thirty minutes, then filter the addresses that appear in your asset inventory and in approved vendor lists. Scope the rule to servers and to privileged accounts first, because developer laptops create the most noise. Add a filter for known content delivery and update services. If you restrict the rule to privileged accounts only, you lose visibility of a low privilege host that an attacker has already taken over, so keep a low severity version running across the whole estate.
